newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Olivetti jobs at risk, no state aid.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Olivetti jobs at risk, no state aid.

text.p: Unions at troubled information technology group Olivetti are fretting over looming job losses but both the ailing company and Italy's government are adamant that state aid is not on the table.

Financial analysts said on Tuesday that if the company can clarify its financial position and assure the Milan stock market that its debts have not spiralled out of control then the company can start to recover without government handouts.

Prime minister Romano Prodi ruled out state aid for the ailing group last week in a meeting with former Olivetti chairman Carlo De Benedetti and analysts believe the group still has the resources to help itself towards safer ground.
"We are staring into a black hole at the moment. But if the company can draw a line under its debt then Olivetti can recover," said one industry analyst in Milan.

Earlier this month, Olivetti reported continued losses for the first half of 1996 and deeper debts, while a former director general in charge of finance and auditing Renzo Francesconi resigned after casting doubts on the accuracy of the accounts.
Trade union leaders agreed there was no need for state money at Olivetti, but they called for an industrial policy aimed at defending Italy's position in the information technology field.

"Olivetti is the tenth largest information technology group in the world and carries an important role for Italy's international standing in the sector," said Gianni Italia of one of Italy's three largest engineering unions Fim.
Claudio Sabattini of another major engineering union Fiom warned that the unions could not accept a break-up of Olivetti which could lead to a "very serious conflict".

At risk are some of the 7,000-plus jobs in the group's personal computer and Lexikon office equipment companies, which were highlighted by group chief executive Francesco Caio as likely to take the brunt of any job losses.
Many of the jobs are concentrated around Olivetti's headquarters in the north-western Italian town of Ivrea.

Caio failed to reassure engineering trade union leaders on Monday over the security of jobs in the PC and Lexikon companies, and the leaders left the meeting in a pessimistic mood saying some 5,000 jobs were at risk.

The company and government officials denied this figure but the restructuring announced with the first-half results for 200 billion lire ($131 million) was aimed to "accelerate the reduction of its presence in the hardware sector" -- meaning two Olivetti companies, PCs and Lexikon.

In the six years up to the end of 1995, Olivetti halved its information technology workforce with the loss of 29,000 jobs, while heavy investment in the mobile and fixed line telecoms business has only created some 3,000 jobs.

Italy's north west area around Turin has shed many industrial jobs in recent years, and Olivetti's last massive restructuring announced last September trimmed 5,000 jobs from a 33,000 workforce -- with PCs and Lexikon the main casualties.

The struggling personal computers company, largely based at Scarmagno near Ivrea, has halved its workforce over the last year to around 1,800 but still Olivetti says it will not even break even in 1996 after it lost some 200 billion lire in 1995.
Lexikon, which makes printers and faxes, has a workforce of 5,500 and is profitable, but a plan to float 40 percent of the group on the U.S. stock market appears to have been put on ice.

Caio's strategy is to focus on three Olivetti companies in the group -- Omnitel mobile phones, Telemedia fixed-line telecoms and its Systems and Services unit, while looking for alliances for its PCs and Lexikon companies. ($1=1,526 lire)
